l: the oath concerning the letter, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHOR. I deplore thee now destined to the gory streams of the lustral
s: Pylades swears to give Iphigenia's letter to her friends, invoking Zeus, while Iphigenia swears by the Goddess Artemis to send him safely beyond the Cyanean rocks. Pylades adds that the oath will not bind him if the vessel and letter are lost in a storm while he survives, but Iphigenia makes him learn the message by heart as well.

l: letter from Iphigenia, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHOR. I deplore thee now destined to the gory streams of the lustral
s: Iphigenia's letter is addressed to Orestes and says that the woman sacrificed at Aulis, Iphigenia, is alive. It asks Orestes to bring her from the barbarian land before she dies and explains that the Goddess saved her by substituting a hind.

l: hind, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHOR. I deplore thee now destined to the gory streams of the lustral
s: The hind is the animal that the Goddess gave in exchange for Iphigenia at the sacrifice. Agamemnon sacrificed it while believing that he was sacrificing Iphigenia.

l: family curse of the Tantalids, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHOR. I deplore thee now destined to the gory streams of the lustral
s: The unit recalls the conflict between Atreus and Thyestes concerning the golden lamb. Orestes also says that he will become a source of curses upon his house if Iphigenia does not remove him from the barbarian land.

l: the fate of Orestes and Pylades, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, CHOR. I deplore thee now destined to the gory streams of the lustral
s: Orestes expects to die in the sacrifice, while Pylades initially declares that he will die with him rather than return alone. Their situation changes when Iphigenia recognizes Orestes as her brother and arranges for Pylades to carry her letter and help secure their escape.

l: The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, IPH. O dearest one, no more, for thou art dearest. I hold thee, Orestes,
s: Iphigenia and Orestes recognize one another as siblings after Orestes, Pylades, and the chorus arrive in the barbarian land. Orestes recounts his mother’s killing, the Erinnyes’ persecution, his trial at the hill of Mars, and Phoebus’s command to seize Diana’s image and take it to Athens. Iphigenia and Orestes devise a plan to claim that Orestes and Pylades are polluted and must be purified at the sea, allowing them to carry away the image and escape by ship. The chorus agrees to keep the plan secret, while Iphigenia mourns Greece and anticipates returning with her brother.

l: Iphigenia, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, IPH. O dearest one, no more, for thou art dearest. I hold thee, Orestes,
s: Iphigenia recognizes Orestes as her long-lost brother and rejoices that he has survived. She recalls the sacrifice arranged by her father and fears that she, Orestes, and Pylades may be discovered, but devises a plan to escape with them and Diana’s image.

l: Orestes, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, IPH. O dearest one, no more, for thou art dearest. I hold thee, Orestes,
s: Orestes embraces Iphigenia and tells her that he is an exile from Argos because the Erinnyes pursue him after he killed his mother. He explains his trial at the hill of Mars and Phoebus’s command that he seize Diana’s image and take it to Athens.

l: Pylades, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, IPH. O dearest one, no more, for thou art dearest. I hold thee, Orestes,
s: Pylades urges Iphigenia and Orestes to stop mourning and concentrate on securing their escape. He is included in the plan as another person polluted by the killing and is to accompany Orestes on the ship.

l: Diana, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, IPH. O dearest one, no more, for thou art dearest. I hold thee, Orestes,
s: Diana’s image is kept in the temple, and Phoebus has commanded Orestes to seize it and carry it to Athens. Iphigenia plans to say that both the strangers and the image must be purified at the sea.

l: Apollo, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, IPH. O dearest one, no more, for thou art dearest. I hold thee, Orestes,
s: Phoebus sent Orestes to Athens for judgment, testified on his behalf at the hill of Mars, and saved him in the trial. He later commanded Orestes to come to the barbarian land, seize Diana’s image, and take it to Athens.

l: Furies, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, IPH. O dearest one, no more, for thou art dearest. I hold thee, Orestes,
s: The Erinnyes pursued Orestes after he killed his mother and drove him through unsettled wanderings. At the hill of Mars, the eldest Erinnyes opposed him in judgment, while others continued persecuting him after the trial until Phoebus’s command gave him hope of release.

l: the Chorus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, IPH. O dearest one, no more, for thou art dearest. I hold thee, Orestes,
s: The chorus witnesses the reunion and agrees to keep Iphigenia’s escape plan secret. It mourns its separation from Greece and imagines Iphigenia returning there by ship.

l: Mycenae, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, IPH. O dearest one, no more, for thou art dearest. I hold thee, Orestes,
s: Iphigenia addresses Mycenae as her dear country and says that it trained Orestes, her brother, in her home. She hopes to restore her ancestral house and return there with Orestes.

l: Argos, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, IPH. O dearest one, no more, for thou art dearest. I hold thee, Orestes,
s: Iphigenia wants to send Orestes back to Argos, and Orestes says that he is exiled from it. He reports that Menelaus rules Argos.

l: Athens, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, IPH. O dearest one, no more, for thou art dearest. I hold thee, Orestes,
s: Athens is the place where Orestes was tried at the hill of Mars and where the sentence released him from the charge pursued by the Erinnyes. Phoebus commands that Diana’s image be taken to Athens.

l: Greece, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, IPH. O dearest one, no more, for thou art dearest. I hold thee, Orestes,
s: Greece is the homeland to which Iphigenia longs to return with Orestes. The chorus also longs for Greek assemblies and describes the ship’s planned journey toward Greece.

l: Tauris, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, IPH. O dearest one, no more, for thou art dearest. I hold thee, Orestes,
s: The barbarian land is where Iphigenia serves as priestess and where Diana’s image is kept. Iphigenia and Orestes plan to escape from it by taking the image to the ship.

l: Iphigenia’s sacrifice at Aulis, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, IPH. O dearest one, no more, for thou art dearest. I hold thee, Orestes,
s: Iphigenia remembers that her father laid a sword on her neck and led her, without a marriage, toward a fictitious wedding with Achilles. She recalls the tears, lamentations, and lustral waters at the altar.

l: Clytæmnestra's murder, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, IPH. O dearest one, no more, for thou art dearest. I hold thee, Orestes,
s: Orestes refers to killing his mother in revenge for his father and declines to discuss the deed in detail. He says that the memory of it caused his exile and persecution by the Erinnyes.

l: Orestes' trial at the Areopagus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, IPH. O dearest one, no more, for thou art dearest. I hold thee, Orestes,
s: Orestes describes standing trial at the hill of Mars, where he and the eldest Erinnyes presented their cases. Phoebus testified for him, Pallas cast the equal deciding votes, and Orestes won the bloody trial.

l: the Erinnyes’ persecution of Orestes, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, IPH. O dearest one, no more, for thou art dearest. I hold thee, Orestes,
s: After Orestes killed his mother, the Erinnyes pursued him through repeated wanderings and caused him to be regarded as frantic. Even after the trial, those who rejected its judgment continued driving him until he returned to Phoebus’s sanctuary.

l: the oracle’s command to seize the image, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, IPH. O dearest one, no more, for thou art dearest. I hold thee, Orestes,
s: Phoebus’s oracle commands Orestes to come to the barbarian land, seize the heaven-sent image of Diana, and place it in Athens. Orestes believes that obeying this command will end his madness and allow him to return to Mycenae.

l: the escape plan, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, IPH. O dearest one, no more, for thou art dearest. I hold thee, Orestes,
s: Iphigenia will tell the king that Orestes and Pylades are polluted and cannot be sacrificed until they are purified at the sea. She will claim that the image was touched by them and must also be washed, then carry it to the ship herself while the others help preserve the secret.

l: temple of Artemis, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, IPH. O dearest one, no more, for thou art dearest. I hold thee, Orestes,
s: The temple contains Diana’s image and has sacred keepers who would prevent Orestes and his companions from hiding inside unnoticed. Iphigenia plans to remove the image from the temple under the pretext of purification.

l: ship, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, IPH. O dearest one, no more, for thou art dearest. I hold thee, Orestes,
s: The ship lies at anchor and is ready for sailing. Iphigenia plans to carry Diana’s image aboard it with Orestes and Pylades so that they can escape the barbarian land and return toward Greece.

l: The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THOAS. Where is the Grecian woman who keeps the gate of this temple? Has
s: Iphigenia pretends that Orestes and the other stranger are polluted by matricide and leads them, with the sacred image of Artemis, toward escape from Tauris. A messenger reports that Iphigenia and Orestes have reached the Grecian ship, but the vessel is driven back by rough water before Minerva appears and calms the sea. Minerva commands Orestes to take Iphigenia and the image to Athens, where the image is to be enshrined, while Iphigenia is to become guardian of Artemis's temple at Brauron. Thoas accepts the goddess's command, releases the Grecian women, and abandons pursuit.

l: Iphigenia, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THOAS. Where is the Grecian woman who keeps the gate of this temple? Has
s: Iphigenia tells Thoas that the sacred image has turned away because the two strangers bear the pollution of matricide. She pretends to purify them and the image, orders that the strangers be taken to the shore, and escapes with Orestes and the image. Minerva commands her to become guardian of the temple of the Goddess at Brauron.

l: Orestes, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THOAS. Where is the Grecian woman who keeps the gate of this temple? Has
s: Orestes is identified as the son of Agamemnon and the brother of Iphigenia, whom she has consecrated to the Goddess at the Tauric altars. He escapes with Iphigenia and the sacred image, fights with the men sent to stop them, and attempts to sail away. Minerva orders him to take Iphigenia and the image to Athens.

l: Thoas, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THOAS. Where is the Grecian woman who keeps the gate of this temple? Has
s: Thoas initially orders the strangers to be purified and guarded, believing Iphigenia's account of their pollution. After learning that Iphigenia and Orestes have escaped, he orders pursuit, but Minerva commands him to stop. He accepts the divine command and allows the fugitives and the Grecian women to depart.

l: Minerva, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THOAS. Where is the Grecian woman who keeps the gate of this temple? Has
s: Minerva appears when Thoas is preparing to pursue the fugitives. She reveals that Orestes came to Tauris by the destined oracles of Loxias and commands him to take Iphigenia and the sacred image to Athens. She also orders that Iphigenia guard the temple at Brauron and that the Grecian women be released.

l: Diana, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THOAS. Where is the Grecian woman who keeps the gate of this temple? Has
s: Artemis is the Goddess whose temple and sacred image are in Tauris. Her image is said to turn away and close its eyes because of the strangers' pollution, but Minerva commands that it be carried to Athens and enshrined there as the Tauric Goddess Diana.

l: the Chorus, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THOAS. Where is the Grecian woman who keeps the gate of this temple? Has
s: The chorus supports Iphigenia's statements and remains involved in the deception concerning the strangers' purification. A messenger accuses the women of sharing in the escape, but they deny responsibility and urge him to find Thoas. Minerva later commands that they be allowed to depart from Tauris.

l: ship, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THOAS. Where is the Grecian woman who keeps the gate of this temple? Has
s: The Grecian ship waits secretly near the shore with its sailors and receives Iphigenia, Orestes, and the sacred image. Men sent by Thoas try to stop it, but the ship's sailors resist them. The vessel is first driven back by strong currents and later is made safe by Minerva's command.

l: Diana's image, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THOAS. Where is the Grecian woman who keeps the gate of this temple? Has
s: The sacred image turns away from its seat and closes its eyes when the strangers approach, which Iphigenia interprets as a sign of pollution. She carries it from the temple under the pretense of purification, and Orestes and Iphigenia take it aboard the Grecian ship. Minerva commands that it be enshrined at Athens.

l: temple of Artemis, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THOAS. Where is the Grecian woman who keeps the gate of this temple? Has
s: The temple is where Iphigenia serves as the woman who keeps the gate and performs sacrifices for the Goddess. She claims that the temple and its image must be purified because of the strangers' pollution. Minerva later directs that the sacred image be removed and enshrined in Athens, while Iphigenia is assigned to guard the Goddess's temple at Brauron.

l: Tauris, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THOAS. Where is the Grecian woman who keeps the gate of this temple? Has
s: Tauris is the barbarian land from which Iphigenia, Orestes, the sacred image, and the Grecian women seek to depart. Thoas commands its people to pursue the fugitives, but Minerva orders him to stop and permits the strangers and women to leave.

l: Greece, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THOAS. Where is the Grecian woman who keeps the gate of this temple? Has
s: Greece is the land from which Orestes and the other stranger have been driven after committing matricide. Iphigenia expresses hatred toward Greece for having destroyed her, yet she uses news from Greece to recognize Orestes and ultimately escapes there with him.

l: Athens, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THOAS. Where is the Grecian woman who keeps the gate of this temple? Has
s: Athens is the destination appointed by Minerva for Orestes, Iphigenia, and the sacred image. The image is to be enshrined there, and Minerva says that she will accompany and protect the travelers.

l: matricide, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THOAS. Where is the Grecian woman who keeps the gate of this temple? Has
s: The two strangers are said to have killed their mother by a conspiracy with the sword. Iphigenia uses this matricide as the pretext for declaring them polluted and arranging their supposed purification.

l: the planned sacrifice of Orestes, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THOAS. Where is the Grecian woman who keeps the gate of this temple? Has
s: Thoas expects Iphigenia to begin the sacrifice of the strangers in the temple. Iphigenia instead falsely presents the sacrifice as a purification and uses the occasion to lead the strangers to the shore and help them escape.

l: purification, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THOAS. Where is the Grecian woman who keeps the gate of this temple? Has
s: Iphigenia claims that the strangers and the sacred image require purification because of the stain of matricide. She orders sea water, fire, lamps, lambs, fetters, and other ritual objects, but the purification is only a deception intended to conceal the escape.

l: escape of Iphigenia and Orestes, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THOAS. Where is the Grecian woman who keeps the gate of this temple? Has
s: Iphigenia arranges the escape by claiming that Orestes and the other stranger must be purified away from the temple. At the shore, she releases them and boards the Grecian ship with Orestes and the sacred image. The escape is challenged by Thoas's men and rough water, but Minerva ultimately ensures that it succeeds.

l: voyage to Athens, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, THOAS. Where is the Grecian woman who keeps the gate of this temple? Has
s: The voyage begins when Iphigenia, Orestes, and the sacred image board the Grecian ship. The ship is driven back by a strong tide and approaches the rocks, but Minerva commands the sea to become calm and directs the vessel toward Athens.

l: The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, notes
s: The unit consists of critical and explanatory notes on Euripides’ Iphigenia in Tauris, including the play’s plot, textual problems, mythological references, and proposed emendations. It discusses Iphigenia’s intended sacrifice at Aulis, her removal through the air by divine agency, and her service as a priestess in Tauris. It also treats Orestes’ wanderings, his encounter with Iphigenia, and the escape from Tauris, while repeatedly evaluating the Cambridge editor’s readings. The notes compare passages in the play with works by Aeschylus, Sophocles, Ovid, Virgil, and other authors.

l: Iphigenia in Tauris, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, notes
s: The unit provides extensive notes on the play’s plot, language, textual transmission, mythological background, and staging. It concerns Iphigenia’s position in Tauris, Orestes’ arrival and escape, and the later intervention of Minerva.

l: Euripides, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, notes
s: Euripides is identified as the author whose Iphigenia in Tauris is being annotated. The notes defend or question various lines attributed to him and compare the play with other works by him, including Orestes, Electra, Hecuba, and Iphigenia in Aulis.

l: Iphigenia, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, notes
s: Iphigenia is described as referring to her intended sacrifice and to Aulis as a place made famous by it. She is carried through the air by divine agency, becomes a priestess in Tauris, recognizes Orestes, sends a letter intended for Mycenae, and participates in the escape plan.

l: Orestes, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, notes
s: Orestes is associated with wanderings, pollution, and the need for purification after his earlier actions. In the play he reaches Tauris, is recognized by Iphigenia, and escapes with her.

l: The Cambridge editor, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, notes
s: The Cambridge editor repeatedly proposes readings, omissions, rearrangements, and explanations for difficult or corrupt passages. The notes praise the editor’s judgment, taste, and treatment of the choruses, while sometimes declining to follow particular suggestions.

l: Aulis, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, notes
s: Aulis is the place where Iphigenia was intended to be sacrificed. The notes describe its recesses as having gained fame through that intended sacrifice and state that Iphigenia was conveyed away from it.

l: Tauris, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, notes
s: Tauris is the setting in which Iphigenia serves as a priestess and where Orestes arrives. The notes discuss the plan by which Iphigenia and Orestes escape from Tauris.

l: Diana, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, notes
s: Artemis is connected with the divine removal of Iphigenia from Aulis and with the altar to which a victim is led. One note refers to the title Trivia in connection with the immolating altar.

l: human sacrifice, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, notes
s: The notes compare the human sacrifice in the play with reported sacrifices among Carthaginians, Gauls, and other peoples. They describe victims being offered through fire or at an altar and discuss the religious and mythological parallels.

l: Iphigenia’s sacrifice at Aulis, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, notes
s: The sacrifice of Iphigenia is treated as an intended sacrifice at Aulis rather than an accomplished death. The notes state that she was conveyed away through the air and connect this event with later references to her supposed death.

l: Orestes’ exile, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, notes
s: The wanderings of Orestes are explicitly noted and linked to his condition after his earlier crimes. The notes refer readers to an explanatory discussion of these wanderings and to Orestes’ eventual arrival in Tauris.

l: escape of Iphigenia and Orestes, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, notes
s: The escape from Tauris involves Iphigenia and Orestes and is discussed through numerous nautical and staging notes. The comments describe preparations involving the ship, oars, ropes, rocks, and measures intended to prevent the vessel from being wrecked.

l: altar, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, notes
s: The altar appears as the place toward which victims are led for sacrifice. The notes also compare the play’s sacrificial altar with descriptions of ritual killing in other ancient sources.

l: letter from Iphigenia, The Tragedies of Euripides, Volume I, notes
s: The letter from Iphigenia is said to begin with a reference to her having been sacrificed at Aulis. It was intended for a cenotaph at Mycenae because she believed she was about to die at Aulis, and the notes clarify that it was sent with that purpose.

l: Alcestis, Alcestis, INTRODUCTION
s: The unit interprets Euripides’ Alcestis as a pro-satyric drama that adapts a traditional story of Alcestis’s sacrifice and Heracles’s rescue of her from Death. It argues that the play refines a formerly broad and comic Satyr-play tradition into a pathetic comedy with delicate psychological treatment. Admetus is presented as generous and affectionate but selfish and self-deceiving, while Alcestis is devoted, practical, and chiefly concerned with her husband and children. Heracles retains the character of a heroic reveller as he feasts, sobers, and wrestles with Death, and the play ends in rejoicing rather than in conventional tragedy.

l: Alcestis, Alcestis, INTRODUCTION
s: The play is described as one of Euripides’ most characteristic and delightful dramas, though it is doubtful whether it should be called a tragedy. It was produced as the fourth play of a series, taking the place of a Satyr-play, and its pro-satyric form helps explain its mixture of tragic diction, pathos, comedy, and rejoicing.

l: Euripides, Alcestis, INTRODUCTION
s: Euripides accepts the traditional story of Alcestis and Heracles but subjects its characters to close psychological analysis. He transforms a broadly comic or Satyric plot into a refined and pathetic comedy, treating its figures delicately while retaining a faint touch of satire or amusement.

l: Admetus, Alcestis, INTRODUCTION
s: Admetus is portrayed as generous, innocent, artistic, affectionate, eloquent, impulsive, spoiled, unconsciously insincere, and fundamentally selfish. He accepts Alcestis’s sacrifice, blinds himself with beautiful words, and is publicly shamed by the Chorus, the Handmaid, and Pheres; after her burial, he recognizes that he sacrificed his honour and lost both honour and happiness.

l: Alcestis, Alcestis, INTRODUCTION
s: Alcestis is beautiful, devoted, simple, homely, and practical rather than artistically eloquent. Before dying, she makes Admetus promise to care for their children and never remarry, chiefly because she fears a stepmother might mistreat them; after returning from death, she remains silent as part of her passage back into the world.

l: Heracles, Alcestis, INTRODUCTION
s: Heracles is presented as a heroic reveller who arrives tired, feasts, drinks, and sings before learning of Alcestis’s death. He then becomes sober, goes out to battle Death, wrestles with him, and brings Alcestis home; he remains triumphant, kindly, and wise while still retaining something of the mocking and boisterous Satyric atmosphere.

l: Satyr-play, Alcestis, INTRODUCTION
s: The Satyr-play followed three tragedies and used a traditional saga plot, heroic characters, tragic diction, and a Chorus of Satyrs to create a controlled burlesque clash. Its subjects commonly included heroic figures congenial to revelry, and its tradition connects joy, nature, Dionysus, the renewal of the earth, and the resurrection of the dead.

l: Pro-satyric drama, Alcestis, INTRODUCTION
s: A pro-satyric drama is a stage in the refinement of the complete Satyr-play, retaining a normal chorus while including one Satyric or revelling figure. Alcestis is identified as a clear example because it has tragic diction, a traditional saga plot, and Heracles as its central revelling figure.

l: Satyrs, Alcestis, INTRODUCTION
s: Satyrs are attendant daemons of Dionysus who form the revel rout and combine human or divine features with those of animals, especially horses or wild goats. They represent joyous, instinctive creatures unconstrained by law or self-control, expressing both the absurdity of half-drunken revellers and the mysterious joy of wild nature.

l: Alcestis's sacrifice for Admetus, Alcestis, INTRODUCTION
s: Alcestis undertakes to die for Admetus when he is allowed to escape death if another person volunteers in his place. Her sacrifice is presented as a response to the danger of Admetus’s death and, according to the suggested interpretation, as a way to protect their children from being left fatherless; she also tries to protect them from a future stepmother by making Admetus promise never to remarry.

l: Heracles's contest with Death, Alcestis, INTRODUCTION
s: After learning that Alcestis has died, Heracles goes out and wrestles with Death, conquering him and bringing Alcestis back. The contest has a half-grotesque and half-ghastly quality, taking place amid graves with the cracking of ribs; Death is treated not as a great Olympian power but as a servant of Hades sent to fetch appointed victims.

l: Alcestis, Alcestis, ALCESTIS
s: Apollo explains that Admetus was spared from death because Alcestis agreed to die in his place, but Thanatos comes to claim her. Alcestis prepares for death, says farewell to Admetus and their two children, and dies after asking Admetus not to take another wife or bring a stepmother into the house. Admetus promises to honor her, mourn her for the rest of his life, and arrange a great funeral. Apollo foretells that Heracles will come and wrest Alcestis from Thanatos, but this has not yet happened in the unit.

l: Admetus, Alcestis, ALCESTIS
s: Admetus is the King of Pherae whose life was previously spared when Alcestis agreed to die in his place. He grieves over Alcestis, promises never to remarry, accepts responsibility for their children, and orders extensive mourning and funeral honors for her.

l: Alcestis, Alcestis, ALCESTIS
s: Alcestis, Admetus's wife and the daughter of Pelias, gives her life to save Admetus. Before dying, she asks him to care for their children and not bring another wife or stepmother into the household.

l: Heracles, Alcestis, ALCESTIS
s: Apollo says that Heracles is coming at the command of a southland king to fetch four wild horses. Apollo foretells that Heracles will wrest Alcestis from Thanatos and the dead.

l: Apollo, Alcestis, ALCESTIS
s: Apollo recounts that he once served Admetus and secured his release from death by arranging that another living person could die in his place. He confronts Thanatos, predicts Heracles's arrival, and leaves before Alcestis dies.

l: Death, Alcestis, ALCESTIS
s: Thanatos comes to the Castle of Admetus to claim Alcestis and refuses Apollo's request to delay her death. He insists on his rights over her and enters the house to place his sword upon her.

l: the two children of Admetus and Alcestis, Alcestis, ALCESTIS
s: The two children follow Alcestis as she leaves the house and say farewell to her. Alcestis entrusts them to Admetus, and he promises to care for them after her death.

l: the little boy, Alcestis, ALCESTIS
s: The little boy runs to Alcestis after she dies and asks why she has gone away, touching her face and calling to her. He tells Admetus that he and his little sister are lonely and cold without their mother.

l: the Handmaid of Admetus, Alcestis, ALCESTIS
s: The Handmaid comes from the Castle of Admetus in tears and describes Alcestis's preparations for death, her prayers, farewells, and final suffering. She tells the Chorus that Alcestis is dying and then returns inside.

l: Chorus, Alcestis, ALCESTIS
s: The Chorus waits outside the Castle of Admetus, fears Alcestis's death, and praises her as the bravest and truest of wives. It prays for help, mourns her death, and urges Admetus to endure the grief that follows.

l: Pherae, Alcestis, ALCESTIS
s: Pherae is the realm of Admetus, whose citizens and elders mourn Alcestis. Admetus orders the people of Pherae to wear mourning and forbids music and celebration for twelve moons.

l: Hades, Alcestis, ALCESTIS
s: Hades is described as the realm beneath the earth to which Thanatos takes the dead. Alcestis imagines the boat and Ferryman of the Dead carrying her toward its palaces.

l: the Castle of Admetus, Alcestis, ALCESTIS
s: The Castle of Admetus is the setting for Alcestis's final preparations, death, and mourning. Apollo watches it, Thanatos enters it to claim Alcestis, and her body is carried from it for burial.

l: Alcestis's death, Alcestis, ALCESTIS
s: Alcestis dies after giving her final instructions and farewells to Admetus and their children. Her death leaves Admetus, the children, the Handmaid, and the Chorus in profound grief.

l: Alcestis's sacrifice for Admetus, Alcestis, ALCESTIS
s: Alcestis sacrifices herself because no other person willing to die for Admetus can be found. She says that she has given him her youth and all her happiness, and that she dies because she could not live separated from him and their children.

l: Admetus's bargain with Death, Alcestis, ALCESTIS
s: Admetus's life was spared through a bargain in which another living soul had to die in his place. Alcestis becomes the person who fulfills that condition after Admetus's father and mother refuse to do so.

l: Alcestis's funeral and burial, Alcestis, ALCESTIS
s: After Alcestis dies, Admetus orders that she receive an honorable funeral and that the whole realm mourn her. Mourners carry her body into the house, and Admetus follows it while preparing further burial honors.

l: grief and mourning, Alcestis, ALCESTIS
s: Grief fills the Castle of Admetus as Admetus, the children, the Handmaid, the servants, and the Chorus respond to Alcestis's death. Admetus orders mourning throughout Pherae, including mourning clothes, shorn horse manes, and the silence of musical instruments for twelve moons.

l: Alcestis, Alcestis, CHORUS.
s: The chorus bids farewell to the Daughter of Pelias, who has died and entered the Sunless Houses. It praises her as a queen among women because she died in another’s stead and became a model of devotion to her lord. The elders condemn his aged parents for refusing to die for him and express admiration for the bride’s sacrifice. They also hope that no later bride will replace her.

l: Alcestis, Alcestis, CHORUS.
s: The Daughter of Pelias is praised after her death as a queen of women and a spouse of spouses. She was unafraid to die, rose up for her lord, and entered the realm of the hungry dead in another’s stead.

l: Admetus, Alcestis, CHORUS.
s: The husband is identified as the son whose mother and father were asked to act for him but dared not do so. His bride died in his place, and the elders say that any new bride after her would be hated by his two children and by them.

l: Sunless Houses, Alcestis, CHORUS.
s: The underworld is called the Sunless Houses and is described as a realm of darkness, tears, and hungry dead. A cold grey-handed guide steers the shadows across its waters, while the weak oar struggles through night and water.

l: Chorus, Alcestis, CHORUS.
s: The chorus praises the Daughter of Pelias and imagines that the dead, minstrels, and singers will proclaim her fame. Its leaders also grieve that they cannot reach or save her, while the elders honor her sacrifice and condemn the failure of her husband’s parents.

l: Alcestis's death, Alcestis, CHORUS.
s: Her death is presented as a deed worthy of lasting song and fullness of fame. She dies for her lord, goes alone to the hungry dead, and is mourned as a uniquely courageous and loving bride.

l: marriage and conjugal devotion, Alcestis, CHORUS.
s: Marriage is portrayed as a bond in which two hearts remain one-knit forever. The Daughter of Pelias exemplifies conjugal devotion by dying for her lord, and the elders call such a bride rare in the world.

l: Alcestis, Alcestis, [_As the song ceases there enters a stranger, walking strongly, but
s: Heracles arrives at Admetus's house while Alcestis is being taken to her burial, but Admetus conceals the identity of the dead woman and welcomes him as a guest. After Alcestis's funeral procession leaves, Admetus quarrels bitterly with his father Pheres over Pheres's refusal to die in his son's place. Heracles feasts without knowing the truth until the Servant reveals that Alcestis is dead, whereupon Heracles resolves to retrieve her from Death and return her to Admetus. The unit emphasizes Admetus's hospitality, the pain and blame surrounding Alcestis's death, and the uncertainty and inevitability of mortal life.

l: Heracles, Alcestis, [_As the song ceases there enters a stranger, walking strongly, but
s: Heracles comes to Pherae while traveling to Thrace to seize Diomede's man-eating horses for the Argive King. Admetus welcomes him despite the funeral in the household, and Heracles feasts without knowing that Alcestis is the dead woman. When the Servant reveals the truth, Heracles is horrified and sets out to rescue Alcestis from Death.

l: Admetus, Alcestis, [_As the song ceases there enters a stranger, walking strongly, but
s: Admetus conceals Alcestis's identity and welcomes Heracles into his house because he refuses to turn away a guest, even during his mourning. He accompanies Alcestis's funeral and violently quarrels with Pheres, condemning him for refusing to die in his son's place. After Pheres leaves, Admetus collapses into grief and goes with the funeral procession.

l: Alcestis, Alcestis, [_As the song ceases there enters a stranger, walking strongly, but
s: Alcestis has died in accordance with her promise to save Admetus's life. She is praised as a faithful, generous, and noble wife who was loved by the household and protected the servants from Admetus's anger.

l: Pheres, Alcestis, [_As the song ceases there enters a stranger, walking strongly, but
s: Pheres comes to Alcestis's burial with gifts and praises her for saving Admetus. Admetus attacks him for refusing to die for his son, but Pheres rejects the accusation, arguing that each person has only one life and that no law requires fathers to die for their sons. He leaves after accusing Admetus of allowing a woman to take his place.

l: the Servant, Alcestis, [_As the song ceases there enters a stranger, walking strongly, but
s: The Servant angrily condemns Heracles for feasting and singing while the household mourns, though he admits that Admetus ordered the grief to be concealed from the guest. He reveals to Heracles that the dead woman is Alcestis and expresses his own love and grief for her.

l: Death, Alcestis, [_As the song ceases there enters a stranger, walking strongly, but
s: Death is imagined as a black, winged lord of corpses who may come to Alcestis's tomb for the blood offered there. Heracles plans either to ambush Death and overpower him or to descend to the underworld and persuade its rulers to surrender Alcestis.

l: Alcestis's funeral and burial, Alcestis, [_As the song ceases there enters a stranger, walking strongly, but
s: Alcestis's body is carried from the house in a funeral procession toward the grave-mound and urn. Admetus asks the citizens to bid her farewell, and Pheres arrives with burial gifts before the procession moves on.

l: Alcestis's death, Alcestis, [_As the song ceases there enters a stranger, walking strongly, but
s: Alcestis's death saves Admetus but leaves the household overwhelmed by grief. Admetus hides the truth of her death from Heracles, while the Servant and the other members of the household mourn her as more than a mistress.

l: Heracles's contest with Death, Alcestis, [_As the song ceases there enters a stranger, walking strongly, but
s: After learning that Alcestis has died, Heracles vows to repay Admetus's hospitality by bringing her back. He intends to confront Death at the tomb or descend to the underworld and use strong prayers to obtain Alcestis's return.

l: hospitality, Alcestis, [_As the song ceases there enters a stranger, walking strongly, but
s: Admetus refuses to turn Heracles away from his house during the mourning and orders that he be given separate rooms, food, and drink. He regards welcoming a stranger as a duty and believes that preserving hospitality will make Heracles his friend rather than leave him friendless in a foreign land.

l: death and mortality, Alcestis, [_As the song ceases there enters a stranger, walking strongly, but
s: Heracles tells the Servant that every mortal must pay the debt of death and cannot know whether life will last another day. The quarrel between Admetus and Pheres shows their conflicting attitudes toward mortality: Admetus condemns Pheres for clinging to life, while Pheres insists that his own life is as precious to him as Admetus's is to Admetus.

l: Alcestis, Alcestis, [_The stage is empty; then_ ADMETUS _and the_ CHORUS
s: Admetus returns to his house grieving Alcestis and declares that life without her is worse than death. The Chorus urges him to endure Fate, while Heracles returns with a veiled woman whom he asks Admetus to shelter. Heracles forces Admetus to take the woman’s hand and reveal her as Alcestis, whom he won from Death after a struggle. Alcestis cannot yet speak and is led into the house, while Heracles departs to continue his labors and Admetus proclaims the household’s renewed happiness.

l: Admetus, Alcestis, [_The stage is empty; then_ ADMETUS _and the_ CHORUS
s: Admetus returns home overwhelmed by Alcestis’s death and fears entering the house, facing the empty bed, chair, and household. He rejects the prospect of another bride, believing that remarriage would dishonor Alcestis, but accepts the veiled woman at Heracles’s insistence and discovers that she is Alcestis restored to life.

l: Chorus, Alcestis, [_The stage is empty; then_ ADMETUS _and the_ CHORUS
s: The Chorus laments Admetus’s loss and tells him that Fate cannot be resisted. It urges him to endure, honors Alcestis’s sacrifice, and concludes that events may unfold beyond human hope or expectation.

l: Heracles, Alcestis, [_The stage is empty; then_ ADMETUS _and the_ CHORUS
s: Heracles returns after winning a woman in contests and asks Admetus to keep her in his house. He reveals that she is Alcestis, whom he recovered by fighting Death, then leaves to continue his task rather than remain for the feast.

l: Alcestis, Alcestis, [_The stage is empty; then_ ADMETUS _and the_ CHORUS
s: Alcestis is brought back veiled and apparently unconscious after Heracles wins her from Death. She resembles her former self but cannot speak until she has completed the required cleansing, and she is led into Admetus’s house.

l: Death, Alcestis, [_The stage is empty; then_ ADMETUS _and the_ CHORUS
s: Death is described as holding Admetus bound to sorrow and as ruling the dead. Heracles fights Death among the dead, grips him as he flees, and takes Alcestis back from his power.

l: Fate, Alcestis, [_The stage is empty; then_ ADMETUS _and the_ CHORUS
s: Fate is portrayed as an irresistible power whose iron grip none can break, not even Zeus’s purposes. The Chorus says that no ritual, philosophy, medicine, or magic can avert what must be.

l: Admetus's house, Alcestis, [_The stage is empty; then_ ADMETUS _and the_ CHORUS
s: Admetus’s house has become a place of grief, with Alcestis’s empty bed, chair, and absence confronting him. At the end, Alcestis is led into the house, and Admetus proclaims that its fortune has been renewed.

l: woman, Alcestis, [_The stage is empty; then_ ADMETUS _and the_ CHORUS
s: The veiled woman is presented by Heracles as a prize won through dangerous contests and is initially intended to become an attendant in Admetus’s house. When unveiled, she is revealed to be Alcestis, not a stranger.

l: Alcestis's death, Alcestis, [_The stage is empty; then_ ADMETUS _and the_ CHORUS
s: Alcestis’s death leaves Admetus grieving, ashamed, and unwilling to enter his house or accept another wife. The Chorus honors her as a woman who died to save her lover and whose name should remain blessed.

l: Alcestis's return to life, Alcestis, [_The stage is empty; then_ ADMETUS _and the_ CHORUS
s: Alcestis returns from the realm of the dead through Heracles’s intervention. She remains silent at first and is taken home to Admetus, who recognizes and embraces the hope of having her again.

l: Heracles's contest with Death, Alcestis, [_The stage is empty; then_ ADMETUS _and the_ CHORUS
s: Heracles says that he fought for life with Death among the dead, springing upon and gripping him as he fled. Through that struggle, he recovered Alcestis for Admetus.

l: Admetus's grief, Alcestis, [_The stage is empty; then_ ADMETUS _and the_ CHORUS
s: Admetus sees his life without Alcestis as worse than death and imagines enduring loneliness, reproach, and the empty household. His grief briefly deepens when the veiled woman resembles Alcestis, but it changes to astonishment and joy when she is revealed.

l: honor and shame, Alcestis, [_The stage is empty; then_ ADMETUS _and the_ CHORUS
s: Admetus fears that people will call him shameful for allowing Alcestis to die in his place and for continuing to live. He insists that remaining unmarried will honor her, and the Chorus holds that Alcestis’s sacrifice deserves lasting honor.

l: Alcestis's sacrifice for Admetus, Alcestis, [_The stage is empty; then_ ADMETUS _and the_ CHORUS
s: Alcestis is remembered as having died to save Admetus, while Admetus regrets that he did not die with her. Her sacrifice is treated as brave, faithful, and worthy of reverence.

l: life and death, Alcestis, [_The stage is empty; then_ ADMETUS _and the_ CHORUS
s: Admetus initially prefers death to a life emptied of Alcestis, while the Chorus insists that human beings must endure what Fate brings. Heracles’s victory over Death transforms the situation, restoring Alcestis to life and renewing Admetus’s faith in Fortune.

l: The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: The document is a sequence of tragic dramas centered on royal families, divine prophecy, honor, burial, deception, and the destructive consequences of pride or inherited violence. In Antigone, Antigone defies Creon’s ban on burying Polynices, invoking Heaven’s unwritten laws; Creon entombs her alive, then reverses himself too late after Tiresias’s warning. Antigone, Haemon, and Eurydicè die, and Creon recognizes his ruin. In Aias, Athena’s madness makes Aias slaughter livestock after Achilles’ armour goes to Odysseus. Ashamed, Aias kills himself; Teucer defends his right to burial against Menelaus and Agamemnon, and Odysseus persuades Agamemnon to permit it. In King Oedipus, Oedipus seeks Laius’s murderer to end Thebes’s plague, only to discover that he killed Laius and married his own mother, Jocasta. Jocasta hangs herself, Oedipus blinds himself, and Creon takes power. Electra follows Orestes’ return to avenge Agamemnon: a false report of Orestes’ death deceives Clytemnestra and Aegisthus, after which Orestes kills them. The Trachinian Maidens shows Dêanira trying to regain Heracles’ love with a robe treated by Nessus; it tortures Heracles, leading Dêanira to kill herself and Heracles to order his own pyre. In Philoctetes, Odysseus and Neoptolemus seek the abandoned Philoctetes and Heracles’ bow for Troy. Neoptolemus abandons deceit, returns the bow, and Heracles commands Philoctetes to sail to Troy, promising healing and glory. Oedipus at Colonos concludes Oedipus’s story: blind and exiled, he receives protection from Theseus at Colonos, rejects Creon and his sons, curses Eteocles and Polynices to kill each other, and dies mysteriously after entrusting Athens’ future protection to Theseus.

l: Antigone, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Antigone is a young, unmarried daughter of Oedipus, sister of Ismene, Polynices, and Eteocles, and the betrothed of Haemon. She is defined above all by devoted kinship and piety: she cares for, guides, and accompanies her blind father through hardship, and she honors her brothers, urging Polynices to abandon the war that will destroy him and Eteocles. After Oedipus disappears, she mourns him and seeks to return to Thebes. There Creon’s attendants seize her during an earlier conflict, though she is later rescued. When Creon forbids Polynices’ burial, she asks Ismene to share the dangerous task but resolves to act alone if necessary. She buries Polynices, declaring that divine and unwritten heavenly laws outweigh a mortal ruler’s command, and accepts death rather than submit. Condemned by Creon, she is led alive into a stone tomb, grieving that she will have neither marriage nor children. She dies by hanging in the death-chamber; Haemon dies beside her.

l: Ismene, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Ismene is a young daughter of Oedipus and sister of Antigone, Polynices, and Eteocles. Cautious and obedient before stronger authority, she refuses to join Antigone’s plan to bury Polynices, saying that women cannot resist the citizens’ resolve; nevertheless, she offers secrecy, later wishes to share Antigone’s guilt and calamity, and fears life without her sister. She also serves Oedipus faithfully: she secretly informs him, brings news of the conflict between Eteocles and Polynices, reports that the Theban race will seek him because victory depends on him, and performs an offering on his behalf. Accompanied by her trusted slave, she joins Antigone in caring for and preparing Oedipus. After his disappearance, she grieves, longs for death with him, and seeks refuge with Antigone.

l: Creon, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Creon is a Theban prince, son of Menoeceus, brother of Jocasta, husband of Eurydicè, father of Haemon, and uncle of Antigone. Through Jocasta he is Oedipus’s brother-in-law, kinsman, trusted friend, and a third partner in rule. He first appears as an envoy from Thebes: he returns from Delphi with Apollo’s message that Laius’s murderer must be expelled or answered with blood, and he advises Oedipus to summon Tiresias. Oedipus later suspects him of plotting for the throne, but Creon denies it, saying he already shares rule’s benefits without its dangers; Jocasta and the Chorus prevent Oedipus from punishing him. After Oedipus’s fall, Creon serves as regent, succeeds to Oedipus’s former kingship, cares for Oedipus’s children, and commands Oedipus’s banishment with the sons’ consent. Later, sent by Thebans, he tries to bring Oedipus from Colonus to Thebes in order to control his burial. When refused, he has Antigone taken by force, threatens to seize Oedipus, and admits capturing Oedipus’s two children in retaliation for Oedipus’s curses; Theseus compels him to lead the way toward them. As newly ruling king of Thebes after Polynices and Eteocles die, Creon makes state loyalty his highest principle. He grants Eteocles burial honors but forbids burial and mourning for Polynices, threatens disobedience with death, and treats the unauthorized burial as bribery or greed. He interrogates Antigone, rejects Ismene’s shared guilt and Haemon’s objections, and orders Antigone confined in a tomb. Tiresias accuses him of divine pollution. Only after prophecy and the Chorus’s urging does he reverse the decree, resolve to bury Polynices, and free Antigone. The reversal comes too late: Haemon dies, Eurydicè kills herself, and Creon acknowledges that his decree and folly caused the disaster. He calls himself his son’s killer, recognizes his folly too late, and asks to be taken away.

l: Polynices, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Polynices is Oedipus’ elder son and Eteocles’ eldest brother. After banishment from Thebes, he takes refuge in Argos, marries Adrastus’s daughter, and raises an Argive army for the Theban succession conflict. He returns against his native city, leads the army, and dies fighting Eteocles. His corpse is denied burial, mourning, and funeral rites, leaving it exposed and said to pollute the city.

l: Eteocles, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Eteocles, younger son of Oedipus and brother of Polynices, gains the Theban throne with popular support after exiling Polynices and depriving him of his claimed right. Oedipus's curse foretells the brothers' mutual death. Eteocles fights for Thebes, dies in single combat with Polynices, and receives sacred burial honors by Creon's order.

l: Oedipus, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Oedipus is a former king of Thebes, adopted son of Polybus and believed son of Merope, who becomes Jocasta’s husband and the father of Antigone, Ismene, Polynices, and Eteocles. As an infant, he is abandoned at Cithaeron with pierced feet, saved by the Corinthian Shepherd, and named for those feet. Believing Polybus and Merope to be his parents, he receives an oracle at Delphi that he will kill his father and marry his mother, so he flees Corinth. On the road, during a quarrel at a crossroads, he kills Laius and Laius’s attendants without knowing Laius’s identity. He later solves the Sphinx’s riddle, wins Thebes’s approval, marries Laius’s widow Jocasta, and rules as king. When Thebes suffers a plague, Oedipus, firmly allegiant to Apollo and to Laius as a dead sovereign, investigates Laius’s murder to save and purge the city. He vows to find and punish the killer, curses the murderer and any concealers, and initially accuses Tiresias and Creon of conspiracy when Tiresias names him as the polluter. Evidence from Jocasta, the Corinthian Shepherd, and the surviving shepherd reveals that Oedipus is the biological son of Jocasta and Laius. His unwitting killing of Laius and marriage to Jocasta fulfill the prophecies: he is both parricide and husband-son of his mother. After Jocasta’s death, Oedipus blinds himself with her pins, becomes a cursed and blind former ruler, and asks to be exiled from Thebes. He requests that Creon care for his daughters and is taken into the palace.

l: Haemon, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Haemon, Creon’s son and Antigone’s promised bridegroom, values her burial of her brother and pleads with Creon to show reason and mercy because Thebes honors her act. After Creon refuses, Haemon leaves in anger. Found with Antigone dead in the burial vault, he attacks Creon, then dies by his own sword while holding her.

l: Tiresias, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Tiresias is a blind prophet and seer, holy, inspired by sacred Truth, and ruled by Apollo in life and prophetic office. Though outwardly blind and guided by his guide, he possesses divine inward knowledge. He tells Creon that pollution in Thebes and failed sacrifices foretell punishment for entombing Antigone and leaving Polynices unburied. Brought before Oedipus, he identifies and accuses him as Laius’s murderer, foretelling divine curse, blindness, exile, poverty, and revelation of his hidden family identity. Oedipus rejects the prophecy and alleges Creon’s manipulation, but Creon denies it.

l: Zeus, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Zeus is a god, high god, all-ruler, and King of the gods. He is father of Athena and Heracles, decrees the voyage to Troy, and values piety toward the gods above other qualities. Characters invoke him as the supreme authority who sees mortal actions, secures his kingdom, witnesses oaths and prophecies, hears pleas for relief, and is called on to punish wrongdoing. Heracles speaks of Zeus's intentions, while Zeus's promises are linked to the benefit of Oedipus's burial to Athens.

l: Bacchus, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Bacchus, a god and child of Semele, is invoked to bring healing to violently afflicted Thebè, where Bacchae and Thyiads honor him in revelry as he haunts the city and moves over Nyseian height.

l: Chorus of Theban Elders, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: The Chorus of Theban Elders is a group of Theban citizens witnessing the conflict between Antigone and Creon. It begins by celebrating victory and mourning Polynices and Eteocles, acknowledges Creon’s authority while allowing for divine action, then reflects on human limits and inherited suffering. As Antigone’s fate darkens, it questions Creon, counsels reason, mourns her, and urgently urges him to heed Tiresias, free Antigone, and bury Polynices.

l: Theban citizens, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Theban citizens are a group subject to Creon’s royal authority and order, with stoning threatened for disobedience and malcontents said to resent his rule. They suffer a plague marked by death, failed crops, dying cattle, and fruitless labor; Oedipus promises relief by finding Laius’s murderer. Tiresias’s warning links that murderer to a true-born Theban. Later, Thebans are said to send Creon to bring Oedipus back to Thebes, under threat of war.

l: Argive army, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Argive army, raised in Argos and allied with Polynices, forms seven battalions under prominent warriors, surrounds Thebes, and attacks it to support Polynices’s attempt to regain power.

l: watchmen, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Watchmen guard Polynices’ corpse, discover it dust-covered and ritually buried at daylight, fear Creon’s punishment, and are ordered to find the responsible person.

l: Thebes, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Thebes is a city, called first among cities, whose safety and greatness are presented as the chief concern of rule. It is the native and ancestral home of Oedipus, Creon, and Antigone, and is associated with sacred shrines, altars, towers, and its people. It first suffers under the Sphinx, but Oedipus solves the riddle, saves and protects the city, and rules it prosperously. Later it is struck by a devastating plague and by pollution from Laius's murder; sacrifices fail and prayers receive no favor. Oedipus seeks to purge the pollution, but the discovery of his crimes leads to his banishment from Thebes. The city is also bound to the consequences of his fate: it seeks his death in a foreign land, believing this will determine a war's outcome, while Oedipus refuses to return because his presence would serve Theban interests. Under Eteocles, after Polynices is exiled, a succession conflict brings an Argive army against Thebes. The city defeats the assault and is celebrated as victorious and restored to peace, with Creon credited with saving it. Yet Creon's punishment of Antigone divides him from Thebes, whose people mourn her. Polynices' unburied corpse then pollutes the city when animals carry his remains to its altars, provoking failed rites and hostile leagues. Thebes endures violent woe but is invoked as a city upheld and needing healing.

l: Argos, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: supports Polynices [through marriage alliance and military aid] Polynices says that he went to Argos, married Adrastus's child, and raised a friendly army there. He intends to return from Argos after defeating those who hold Theban power.

l: the palace of Laius, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Creon’s royal palace contains the bridal room where Jocasta dies and becomes a site of concealed, unpurgeable horror: Eurydicè emerges from it, Haemon and Eurydicè’s bodies are brought or revealed there, and Oedipus is taken back inside.

l: Creon's proclamation against Polynices' burial, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Creon’s proclamation honors Eteocles’ burial but forbids anyone to bury, mourn, or perform funeral rites for Polynices, leaving his body exposed and threatening death for disobedience. The decree also orders Antigone sealed in a tomb. Though Creon initially rejects divine and prophetic opposition, he resolves to reverse it; he later recognizes it caused disaster, including Haemon’s and Eurydicè’s deaths.

l: the attack on Thebes, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: An Argive assault led by Polynices and seven commanders seeks to take Thebes, recover the throne from Eteocles, destroy the city, burn its shrines, and capture its people. Despite Antigone’s plea, Polynices proceeds; Thebes overcomes the leaders and routs the attackers.

l: the deaths of Polynices and Eteocles, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: The deaths of Polynices and Eteocles are their prophesied mutual killing in single combat during the war against Thebes. Though warned, Polynices proceeds; after conflict between Thebes and Argos, the brothers kill each other, ending their struggle.

l: Polynices' burial, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: is_forbidden_by Creon's proclamation against Polynices' burial [publicly and under penalty of death] Polynices receives burial from an unidentified person despite Creon’s prohibition. The burial consists of dust placed over his body and the religious rites required for the dead.

l: Eteocles' burial, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Eteocles receives lawful, fully honored burial rites: Antigone scatters dust over the body and pours three libations, but guards catch her after uncovering it.

l: Antigone's disobedience, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Antigone’s disobedience is her deliberate defiance of Creon’s command: she buries Polynices, is initially unidentified by the watchman, then openly admits and refuses to regret the act, placing Heaven’s eternal laws and her brother’s burial above mortal authority and death.

l: the conflict between Eteocles and Polynices, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: The conflict is a struggle for the Theban throne between the brothers Eteocles and Polynices. After they initially agree to leave the throne vacant because of their father's pollution, Eteocles deprives Polynices of rule and banishes him. Polynices gains Argive support and invades Thebes, but the doomed Argive attack is defeated and both brothers die.

l: burial rites, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Creon grants Eteocles the full sacred rites appropriate to an honored dead man while denying them to Polynices. The watchman reports that someone has nevertheless performed the required rites for Polynices.

l: loyalty to the state, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: is Creon's governing principle [expressed as devotion to the fatherland] Creon declares that loyalty to the state must take precedence over personal friendship. He promises honor in life and death to those who love Thebes and denies recognition to those he considers enemies.

l: Justice, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Justice is a divine or moral force tied to burial, piety, and judgment. It requires burial for the dead and protects noble dead from hatred. Antigone invokes higher laws and burial duties against Creon, while Clytemnestra claims Justice killed Electra’s father; Electra warns that Justice may later judge her.

l: authority and obedience, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Ismene argues that obedience to authority is necessary because she and Antigone are women and lack power to resist the citizens and the king. Creon demands obedience to his decree and threatens severe punishment for disobedience.

l: Polynices' corpse, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Polynices' corpse is ordered to remain unburied and exposed, suffering dogs and vultures and polluting the altars; later it is found untouched by animals, thinly dust-covered and given the required burial rites.

l: dust covering Polynices' body, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: covers Polynices' corpse [thinly and without a grave] A thin layer of dust has been placed over Polynices’ body by someone who left no identifiable trace. The dust is presented as part of the burial act that violates Creon’s order.

l: grave, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: The watchman reports that Polynices is not in a grave. Instead, the body lies with dust covering it and with the required religious rites performed.

l: Mankind, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Mankind is a mortal being of extraordinary, inventive skill: through labor it subdues Earth, sails the sea, captures and tames animals, and possesses wise speech and swift thought. It creates cities, shelter, and cures, but its resourcefulness may serve good or evil, and it cannot escape Death.

l: the Gods, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: The Gods are the divine power governing moral and human fate. They establish eternal, unwritten law above mortal edicts, observe righteousness and wrongdoing, and require reverence and protection for suppliants. They inflict recurring suffering and inherited doom on the house of Cadmus, reject polluted sacrifices in Thebes, and punish violence against the dead and living. They abhor Oedipus as accursed, though his end must be determined by their will. Through thunder, lightning, and divine voices, they announce his appointed end; guided by Hermes and the Queen of realms below, he disappears and is received after death.

l: Death, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: is_a deity [Antigone's only deity in the tomb] Antigone says that Death is the one fate from which man cannot obtain reprieve. She accepts death as preferable to abandoning her dead brother and describes Death as the only deity who may spare her soul in the cave-like tomb.

l: the people of Thebes, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: The people of Thebes once regard Oedipus as king and protector, but are later invoked as witnesses to his crimes. Under Creon, they privately praise Antigone’s burial of her brother and condemn her death sentence, yet fear prevents open opposition.

l: the law, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: is_a unwritten law of Heaven [infallible and everlasting] Creon insists that the law and the ruler's commands must be obeyed in great and small matters, whether right or wrong. Antigone distinguishes his published edict from the eternal, unwritten laws of Heaven, which she says his command cannot override.

l: Creon's death sentence against Antigone, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: confines Antigone [alive in a cave-like tomb] Creon confirms that Antigone must die after she admits burying Eteocles and refuses to repent. He decides that she will be hidden alive in a cave-like place with enough food to prevent pollution from reaching the city.

l: the marriage of Antigone and Haemon, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Creon treats Antigone's promised marriage to Haemon as no reason to spare her and says that Haemon may find another bride. Ismene warns that Antigone's death will also destroy the espousal, while Haemon says he knows whom her death will ruin.

l: the cave-like tomb, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: A strong, deep, cave-like sepulchral prison-house, it confines Antigone alive with provisions by Creon’s order, away from human footsteps. Intended to avert the city’s pollution while leaving her fate to Death, the entombment is later called a godless act provoking powers beneath.

l: the dead body of Eteocles, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: The guards uncover the dead body of Eteocles and later catch Antigone covering it again with dust and honoring it with libations. Antigone says that leaving her brother without burial would have been an intolerable sorrow.

l: human suffering and inherited doom, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: afflicts the stock of Cadmus [across successive generations] The Chorus says that the house of Cadmus has suffered woe after woe, with each generation receiving fresh sorrow from those who came before. It compares this inherited calamity to an expanding storm and says that even a brief hope of relief is extinguished by death and fate.

l: Oedipus, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Oedipus is an aged, blind former king of Thebes, son of Laius and descendant of Labdacus. Native to Thebes, he becomes an exile after unknowingly killing his father and marrying his mother, acts for which he is accused despite insisting they were involuntary. Banished and forbidden from Thebes, he wanders with the devoted support of his daughters Antigone and Ismene. At Colonos near Athens, led by Antigone, he enters the sacred grove of the Eumenides as a suppliant and says he brings blessing to those who shelter him. He learns that his sons Eteocles and Polynices are in conflict and seek him because an oracle makes his fate important; he refuses to help them and curses them, especially Polynices for driving him into exile. He seeks Theseus's protection, offers his body and burial as a benefit to Athens, and resists Creon's attempt to seize his daughters. Theseus rescues Antigone and Ismene, earning Oedipus's gratitude. Protected by the gods and guided toward an appointed death, Oedipus recognizes thunder and lightning as its approach. He leads his daughters and Theseus toward a secret resting-place, entrusts Theseus with knowledge that will protect Athens, asks him to guard the daughters, and disappears without visible cause. His death is peaceful and wondrous; his hidden burial is a boon to Athens and inauspicious to his enemies.

l: Jocasta, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Jocasta is Thebes's queen, Creon's sister, Laius's wife, and later Oedipus's wife. With Laius, she bears a son who is abandoned after his feet are bound; believing him dead, she rejects the oracle about Laius's death. She helps halt Oedipus and Creon's quarrel and recounts Laius's killing and the infant's abandonment, prompting Oedipus's suspicions. At first she treats Polybus's death as proof prophecy failed, but, fearing Oedipus's true parentage, begs him to stop the inquiry. When testimony reveals that Oedipus is her son, she grieves over her twofold marriage and hangs herself in the bridal room.

l: Polynices, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Polynices, Oedipus’s elder son and Eteocles’s rival, is exiled from Thebes after being dethroned. In Argos he gains a marriage-based league and leads an army against Thebes to recover his throne. Seeking Oedipus’s aid, he is cursed, accepts death, rejects Antigone’s plea to withdraw, and departs.

l: Antigone's burial, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: is_ordered_by Creon [as confinement alive in a tomb] Antigone is condemned to an unusual living burial rather than an ordinary death. After Tiresias' warning, Creon agrees to release her from the vault.

l: Tiresias' prophecy, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: foretells Creon's ruin [as punishment for his actions] Tiresias prophesies that Creon will soon give a corpse from his own bloodline in payment for Antigone's entombment and Polynices' lack of burial. He also foretells cries of mourning in Creon's palace and enmity from cities whose dead remain unburied.

l: Fate, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Fate is an irresistible force that overcomes mortals, determines human suffering, and brings unavoidable calamity. Wealth, warfare, and seafaring cannot resist it; Creon fears and finally acknowledges its disastrous, dreadful work.

l: Love, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Love is an irresistible force that leads immortals and DÊ at its will, explaining how Heracles and others may be overcome by passion.

l: death, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Death is portrayed as a silent, hidden destination for the condemned: a deep house and eternal bridal chamber for the dead. For Antigone it is a grave fate imposed while she lives; for Aias it is a welcome passage to painless rest. Its aftermath brings grief, danger, uncertainty, and conflict over burial. Electra contrasts desired death with the misery of being unable to die.

l: Athena, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Athena is a goddess, daughter of Zeus, who intervenes in Aias's fate. Angry at his pride and impiety, she prevents his planned attack on the Greek generals by inducing madness and making livestock seem like enemies. She warns Odysseus about unstable fortune and humility, guards him, and later inspires him to accept Aias's funeral. She is said to drive Aias toward destruction if he leaves shelter.

l: Chorus, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Chorus is a group of sailors under Neoptolemus, whom it supports as captain. It portrays Philoctetes’ isolation and urges relief while weighing departure, then defers to Neoptolemus. Calling itself a seer, it says a night vision banishes fear and foretells vengeance. It then prays to Bacchus, asks of Haemon’s death, laments Creon’s ruin, and closes by praising wisdom and piety and condemning pride.

l: Messenger, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: The Messenger reports that Haemon is dead by his own hand after attacking Creon over the murder of the maiden. He describes the burial of Polynices, the discovery of the maiden hanging in the vault, and Haemon dying beside her.

l: second Messenger, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: is_a messenger [reporting to Creon] The second Messenger tells Creon that Eurydicè is dead and that she cursed him after hearing of Haemon’s death. He reports that she wounded herself before the altar.

l: Eurydicè, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Eurydicè, queen of Thebè and mother of Haemon, hears of Haemon’s death, leaves silently, then dies by suicide before the altar, lamenting Megareus and Haemon and cursing Creon.

l: the burial vault, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: contains Antigone [as her stone death-chamber] The burial vault is the maiden’s stony chamber of death. Inside it, the men find her hanging and Haemon alive but grieving; Haemon then dies there beside her.

l: Haemon's corpse, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: is_carried_by Creon [in Creon's arms] Creon enters bearing Haemon’s corpse on his arm. He identifies it as the consequence of his own error and carries it while mourning his son.

l: Haemon's death, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: is_caused_by Creon's decree [through the murder of Antigone] Haemon’s death follows his discovery of the maiden’s body and his confrontation with Creon. He plunges his sword into his side and dies beside the maiden, joined to her in Hades.

l: Eurydice's suicide, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: is_caused_by Haemon's death [after she hears the lamented death] Eurydicè’s suicide occurs after she hears of Haemon’s death. She wounds herself to the heart before the altar and curses Creon for the deaths of his children.

l: the death of Antigone, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: The maiden dies by hanging in the burial vault after being enclosed in her chamber of death. Her death is followed by Haemon’s suicide beside her.

l: rashness, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: is_a evil [the worst evil in mortal life] The Messenger calls rashness the worst evil in mortal life. Haemon’s violent response and Creon’s actions are presented as producing catastrophic consequences.

l: pride, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: is_punished_by sorrow [when it is boastful and excessive] Creon’s pride appears in his earlier authority and in the consequences of his inflexible rule. The Chorus teaches that the proud are brought low and learn their lesson late.

l: piety toward the gods, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Piety to Heaven is a condition of wise conduct and happiness, preserved against pride’s sorrow and enduring after death through human conduct.

l: human happiness and woe, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: is_governed_by Fortune [as Fortune smiles or lowers] The Messenger says that human happiness and woe change as fickle Fortune smiles or darkens. He judges that wealth and royal appearance are nothing without joy.

l: Odysseus, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Odysseus is a Greek, Ithacan, and Achaean commander and king, son of Laërtes, who serves Zeus and acts as a leading strategist for the Achaean expedition. His record presents him as both a hostile rival and a morally complicated leader. In the matter of Aias, he pursues the aftermath of Aias's slaughter of livestock, pities his enemy's divinely caused misery, and recognizes the uncertainty of human life. Though Aias's madness is said to benefit him and others expect him to mock Aias, he later defends Aias's right to burial, persuades Agamemnon to permit it, and offers help to Teucer. In the matter of Philoctetes, Odysseus is remembered as the man who, with the Atridae, abandoned and cast out Philoctetes on Lemnos and who took Achilles' armour. After learning a prophecy that Philoctetes and his bow are needed, he leads the effort to retrieve him. He relies on deceit, directing Neoptolemus to entrap Philoctetes and planning disguise, while also pursuing force. He invokes Zeus and the Achaean army to compel Philoctetes' return and opposes restoring the bow. Yet when threatened with the bow, he withdraws. Across these episodes, he pursues Achaean aims through authority, strategy, deceit, and occasional compassion.

l: Aias, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Aias is a Greek and Argive warrior, son of Telamon, brother of Teucer, lord of the Salaminian Mariners, husband or consort of Tecmessa, and father of Eurysakes. Renowned as the greatest or most valiant surviving Greek, he rescues the Greek ships from Hector, fights Hector in single combat, and bears a seven-hided shield and a sword received from Hector. His central downfall begins when Achilles' armor is awarded to Odysseus: stripped of honor, hostile to the Atreidae, and ashamed before his father, he is driven by Athena into madness. Believing livestock to be the Greek generals and Odysseus, he attacks and slaughters flocks and herds with his sword and bloody scourge. When reason returns, he recognizes the destruction, grieves, and resolves that death is his escape from dishonor. He entrusts Eurysakes, Tecmessa, and his armor to those around him, then leaves carrying his sword under the stated purpose of burying it and purifying himself. In a lonely wooded place, he falls upon the sword and dies, asking that Teucer receive his body and calling for vengeance on the Achaeans. Menelaus and Agamemnon oppose his burial, but Teucer defends his service and Odysseus calls him, apart from Achilles, the noblest Argive at Troy. His funeral rites begin, and the Chorus remembers him as a noble fallen warrior.

l: Tecmessa, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Tecmessa is a captive woman of noble Phrygian lineage, daughter of Teleutas, and Aias’ concubine, housemate, and dependent, though she calls him husband and master. Loving Aias and mother of their son Eurysakes, she fears that his death will leave them enslaved and humiliated. She recounts Aias’ raid, cruelty to animals, and grief after his madness ends, then begs him not to abandon her and their child. Sensing his fatal intent, she seeks him after a warning, finds him dead, mourns him, covers his body, summons Teucer, and brings Eurysakes for burial.

l: Teucer, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Teucer is Telamon’s son, Aias’s brother and defender, an Achaean warrior and skilled archer. While absent in pursuit of enemies, he comes from the Mysian heights with Calchas’s warning that Aias must not go abroad, but arrives after Aias’s death. He mourns, fears Telamon’s anger and exile, and makes Aias’s burial his chief concern. Though Menelaus and Agamemnon forbid burial and insult him over his mother’s captive status, Teucer defends Aias’s worth, recalls his rescue of the army and combat with Hector, and vows resistance. He summons Eurysakes, protects him as guardian, and organizes the cleansing, preparation, and burial of Aias’s corpse.

l: Eurysakes, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Eurysakes, child of Aias, is brought to his father’s body, protected by Teucer, and told to guard it during a burial dispute.

l: Achilles, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Achilles, the greatest Argive warrior except Aias, is Neoptolemus’ father, whose nobility and armour shape his son’s role. Esteemed by Philoctetes, he dies from Phoebus’ shaft; afterward Neoptolemus claims his armour and aids Philoctetes’ victory.

l: Menelaus, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Menelaus, Spartan king and commander of the Greek expedition, is Aias’s enemy. At Aias’s body, he orders Teucer not to tend or bury it, calling Aias a threat to the host; Teucer defies him, and Menelaus leaves.

l: Agamemnon, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Agamemnon is an Achaean lord, king of the Greeks, and commander who leads the Achaean host and navy in the war against Troy. He is Menelaus’s brother and the father of Electra, Chrysothemis, Orestes, and Clytemnestra’s daughter. At Aulis, he sacrifices his daughter so the Greek fleet can sail to Troy, an act later disputed by Clytemnestra and Electra. After Troy, he returns and is murdered by Clytemnestra with Aegisthus, reportedly by a bronzen-grinding axe. His death, tomb, and memory remain central: Electra honors him, the Chorus says he is not forgotten, and Orestes prepares to avenge him. In another conflict, he hates Aias and first refuses Aias burial, but, persuaded by Odysseus, allows Teucer to bury him while maintaining his hatred.

l: Atreidae, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Atreidae are twin, high-sceptred kings and rulers of the Greek army. Their authority and actions provoke hostility: they use craft to award Achilles’ armor to a wit-proud man, depriving Aias and Neoptolemus of it and earning Aias’s enmity. They abandon Philoctetes on Lemnos because of his plague, casting him away and destroying his life. Later, after Helenus’ prophecy, they pursue Philoctetes because he is required for Troy’s capture. Philoctetes fears renewed harm from them, though he must aid their cause.

l: Salaminian Mariners, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: The Salaminian Mariners are Aias’s Greek sailor-companions and chorus. Loyal to him, they fear hostile reports from the Greek army, question Tecmessa, sympathize with Aias, and consider fleeing the Atreidae’s anger. They mourn his ruin, receive his charge to protect Eurysakes, and search for him after danger is reported. Finding Aias dead, they lament their failure to guard him, support Teucer’s burial effort, and grieve Aias, the Trojan War’s hardships, and the loss of their former security.

l: Greeks, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: are_hostile_to Aias [after his disgrace] Aias says that the Greeks have denied his peerless prowess and that he cannot safely return home stripped of his honor. He also says that no Greek should trample Eurysakes after his death, trusting Teucer to protect the child.

l: Achaeans, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: The Achaeans are a host or army at Troy in the Trojan war. They scorn and destroy Aias after the judgment over Achilles' armor, threaten him and attack Teucer, and are to receive Philoctetes. Their generals abandoned Philoctetes, seek his bow for the war, and oppose its return by Neoptolemus.
