l: Salamis, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Salamis is an island, Aias’s ancestral homeland and place of glory, praised amid the waves and admired by the world. Its blessed condition contrasts with sailors’ weary exile. In a lonely wooded place, Aias calls its sacred fields home, bids them farewell before dying, and asks the Sun to report his fall there.

l: Achilles' armour, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Achilles' armour, made by Hephaestus, becomes contested after Achilles' death. Though Aias is most valiant, surviving Greek judges award it to Odysseus as wisest, enraging Aias. Neoptolemus later seeks it, but Odysseus claims he saved it and Achilles; Neoptolemus returns to Scyros deprived.

l: the sword (Aias's sword gifted by Hector), The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Aias's sword, a weapon received from the enemy Hector, is sharp, bloodied in livestock slaughter, and capable of cutting, piercing, hacking, and tearing. Aias says it has brought him no kindness among the Argives and calls it a weapon of hatred. Though he plans to bury it, he carries it away, sharpens and plants it in Trojan soil, then uses it to pierce his heart.

l: the flocks and herds, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: The army's flocks, herds, and herdmen are slaughtered during Aias' night raid. Aias brings some of the surviving animals into his tent, where he treats them as captive Greek commanders and tortures them.

l: Aias's madness, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Aias's madness, attributed to Athena and Pallas, diverts his intended attack on the Greek generals, Odysseus, and the host onto livestock. Deluded, he mistakes bulls, rams, sheep, and other animals for his enemies, raids the army's animals, and slaughters the flocks. When the madness ends, he recognizes the disaster, remains self-alienated and overwhelmed by shame and grief, and the condition is said to bring his ruin and death.

l: Aias' raid on the army's livestock, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Aias raids the army's flocks, herds, and herdmen alone at night, believing he is avenging himself on Greek leaders, and the raid is mistaken for an attack on the generals.

l: the prize-encounter for Pelides' arms, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: The contest for Achilles' arms is the event that opens Aias's great pain. Aias says the Atreidae used deceit to award the armor to Odysseus rather than to him, despite his proven bravery, causing his despair. Neoptolemus calls the award a robbery, chiefly blaming the Atreidae while also condemning Odysseus for accepting it.

l: Aias' attempted attack on the generals, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Aias, enraged by losing Achilles' armour, approaches the generals' tents to kill Greek commanders, but Athena maddens him into attacking livestock instead.

l: honour, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Honour is lost by Aias after Achilles' armour goes to Odysseus and his livestock slaughter, then restored through his honoured funeral.

l: divine madness and fate, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Divine madness and fate govern Aias briefly: Athena redirects his intended violence to livestock, showing divine power and changeable fortune can destroy even a powerful, valiant man.

l: Hector, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Hector is a Trojan warrior and Aias’s most hated enemy. They exchange gifts: Hector gives Aias a sword and receives a girdle. The sword is used by Aias to kill himself; the girdle is used to drag Hector to death.

l: Apollo, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Apollo is a god who speaks through oracles at Pytho and Delphi and directs punishment and investigation. He sends word that Thebes must remove the pollution caused by Laius’s murder: the killers must be found and killed or exiled. His authority supports Tiresias’s prophecy, and the Chorus associates him with perfect sight, sacred rites, and the force of prophecy. Oedipus says Apollo brought about his calamity, including his blindness. Apollo later gives Orestes an oracle commanding punishment for Agamemnon’s murder through deception, guiding disguise, a false death report, and an attack on the palace. He also kills Achilles with an arrow.

l: Troy, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Troy is a region and city near the Greek camp, hostile to Aias and later feared by Teucer as an enduring enemy. Aias, after disgrace, calls the Trojan plain a place that fostered him, considers fighting alone before its walls, and rejects it because the Atreidae might rejoice. It is the city against which the Greeks sailed and the target of the Greek army. Its capture is repeatedly presented as destined but conditional: Helenus says it cannot be taken until Philoctetes returns from Lemnos, and Odysseus says its fall requires Philoctetes’ bow. Neoptolemus is ordered to bring Philoctetes there, though Philoctetes refuses for much of the action. Heracles finally declares that they will go and that Troy will fall before the bow, to the Achaeans at the appointed time.

l: the slaughter of the flocks, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: results_from Aias's madness In his madness, Aias kills horned and bleating animals, believing that he is attacking the men who wronged him. He calls the deed a dark blood-stream and a mockery of his strength, while Tecmessa and the sailors regard it as evidence that his reason was gone.

l: Aias's contemplated suicide, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Aias considers death preferable to living in dishonor and says that noble hearts require honor either in life or in the grave. He later takes his bright sword into the countryside, intending to bury it after purifying himself, while Tecmessa and the sailors race to prevent his death.

l: Aias's exile and dishonor, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: is_caused_by the judgment over Achilles' armor [in Aias's view] Aias feels rejected by the Achaeans and unable to return before his father without the prize of renown. He sees Troy and the camp as hostile, fears the humiliation of facing Telamon, and believes that his disgrace has made continued life unbearable.

l: divine wrath and human pride, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: is_a cause of Aias's fall [as explained by Calchas] Calchas explains Aias's fall through his prideful claims that he could win without the gods and that Athena was unnecessary where he stood. The prophet says that people who think beyond the human measure provoke heaven, and that Athena's anger threatens Aias's life.

l: the Achaean army, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: is_a Greek host [besieging Troy] The Achaean army is described as the force Aias was expected to help. Menelaus claims that Aias tried to attack and kill the host by night, while Aias calls for vengeance on Achaean flesh and the camp.

l: Athens, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Athens is a renowned, mighty Greek city near Colonos, loved by Aias and praised as the mightiest in Hellas. It matters most as a refuge governed by justice, equity, piety, mercy, and law: it shelters sufferers and exiles, honors the Gods, and ratifies nothing apart from the law. Ruled by Theseus, Athens protects Oedipus, his daughters, and Polynices through Theseus and its citizens, upholding friendship, its laws, and its honor. Oedipus comes to trust Athens as the one place where he finds piety, justice, and truth, and he blesses it. In return for Theseus keeping the secret of his resting-place, Oedipus promises Athens lasting protection against future enemies. The record closes with Theseus bound by this oath and promising aid to Oedipus's daughters.

l: the wooded spot, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: is_a lonely place [setting of Aias's suicide and discovery] The scene changes to a lonely wooded spot where Aias plants Hector's sword and kills himself. Tecmessa later finds his body there, concealed within the ground.

l: Aias's corpse, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Aias’s corpse, a dead body found fallen on its sword in a lonely wooded spot, becomes the center of a burial dispute. Initially covered by Tecmessa and denied burial by Agamemnon, it is uncovered and defended by Teucer, who insists it be removed from the blade, receive lawful obsequies, and be prepared for burial.

l: Aias's burial, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Aias’s burial is a contested funeral rite. Menelaus and Agamemnon oppose it, but Teucer defends and undertakes it as justice owed to the dead; Odysseus supports burial under Heaven’s laws. Teucer orders guards and prepares the grave, cleansing water, fire, arms, and attendants.

l: Aias's suicide, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: is_a self-inflicted death [performed with Hector's sword] Aias's suicide follows his despair over his disgrace and suffering. He chooses death with Hector's sword, asks for his body to be protected from enemies and scavengers, and treats death as a passage to rest.

l: the Trojan War, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: The Trojan War is a long, grievous conflict on the Trojan plain, caused by Paris, whom the Chorus blames for teaching the Greeks swords and dense battle lines and thus creating years of wandering, fighting, and suffering. It brings Neoptolemus to Troy, prompts disputes over Achilles’ death and armour, and leads to Philoctetes’ abandonment. As the war continues, the Achaean host seeks Philoctetes and his bow; despite having been abandoned by the generals, he is needed, according to Helenus’ prophecy, to help ravage Troy and secure Greek victory.

l: honor and burial rights, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Menelaus argues that honor forbids granting a tomb to an enemy and that authority must be obeyed for armies and states to function. Teucer rejects this argument and maintains that Aias must be buried, while the Chorus urges him to secure a grave for the valiant dead.

l: Pelops, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: is_a Phrygian [Agamemnon's paternal ancestor] Pelops is associated with the chariot-course that the Chorus describes as burdened by toil.

l: Laius, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Laius is a descendant of Cadmus, son of Labdacus, former king of Thebes, and Jocasta’s husband. He is the biological father of Oedipus and of an infant son abandoned after being given to the Theban Shepherd. While traveling to Delphi with five companions in a chariot, he is killed at a crossroads in Phocis by Oedipus shortly before Oedipus becomes king. His unsolved murder brings pollution and plague to Thebes, leading Apollo’s command that the killer be found and punished.

l: Priest of Zeus, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: is_a priest [arch priest of Zeus] The Priest of Zeus speaks for the suppliants before Oedipus. He describes Thebes as afflicted by pestilence and asks Oedipus to save the city.

l: the Corinthian Shepherd, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: A shepherd from Corinth announces Polybus’s death, gives the foundling Oedipus to Polybus, and reveals Oedipus was received from the Theban Shepherd with pierced feet.

l: the shepherd of Laius, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: The shepherd of Laius, a slave bred in Laius’s house, is the sole surviving witness of Laius’s death and reports the supposed robbers. After seeking exile in rural pastures, he is summoned to testify. He admits Jocasta gave him an infant to destroy; pity led him to give it to the Corinthian Shepherd, confirming it was Laius’s stock.

l: Polybus, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Polybus is the king of Corinth and Oedipus’s believed father. Oedipus flees Corinth to avoid killing him after an oracle. Polybus later dies from sickness and old age, and a Corinthian Shepherd reveals that he adopted, not begot, Oedipus.

l: Sphinx, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: The Sphinx, a hateful destructive songstress, devastates Thebes by devouring failed riddle-solvers until Oedipus solves her riddle and overcomes her.

l: Theban Elders, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: The Theban Elders are a civic chorus of Cadmeans speaking for the Theban people. In a city devastated by plague, deaths, and failed childbirths, they pray to Apollo, Pallas, Artemis, and other gods for relief. They seek the truth about the oracle and Laius’s murder, deny guilt, and urge Oedipus to consult Tiresias and heed the heavenly oracle. Though initially uncertain about Tiresias’s prophecy, they support Oedipus for having saved Thebes from the female monster, help end his quarrel with Creon, and uphold divine laws and prophecies. As the shepherd approaches, they speculate about Oedipus’s origins; after his ruin and blinding, they mourn and declare that no mortal is happy before life ends without sorrow.

l: Train of Suppliants, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: is_a suppliant group [before the altar] The Train of Suppliants kneels before the altar with sacred branches and appeals to Oedipus for aid. Oedipus tells them to rise after promising to answer the city's needs.

l: Cithaeron, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Cithaeron is a mountain wilderness and pasture where Oedipus was exposed, found, and fostered; shepherds grazed flocks there. Remembered as the place where his feet were bound and he was rescued, it becomes the site Oedipus wishes had killed him.

l: Corinth, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Corinth is Oedipus's home region, where he was raised as Polybus and Merope's son and Polybus ruled. He fled it to avoid the oracle that he would kill his father and marry his mother; a Corinthian Shepherd later comes from there.

l: Delphi, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Delphi is an oracle shrine sacred to Apollo and host of the celebrated Delphian games, including foot-races and chariot races. It is sought for prophetic guidance: Creon consults Apollo there about Laius’s murder, and its oracle foretells Oedipus’s acts. The Chorus questions its guidance unless fulfilled, while Orestes wins and competes in its games.

l: oracle of Apollo, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: An oracle from Apollo, given at Pytho, identifies Laius's unresolved murder as the pollution causing Thebes's plague. It commands that the murderers be found and punished by death or exile, and Oedipus uses this instruction to begin his investigation.

l: the prophecy of Oedipus's parentage and crimes, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: The prophecy foretells that Oedipus will kill his father, commit incest with his mother, suffer exile and curses, lose sight after prosperity, and become beggared. Told of this fate, he flees Corinth in fear. Later, after learning that he killed Laius and married Jocasta, he recognizes that the prophecies have been fulfilled.

l: the murder of Laius, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: The murder of Laius, at a crossroads in Phocis where the roads from Daulia and Delphi meet, pollutes Thebes and is to be avenged by punishing those responsible. It was reported as an attack by foreign robbers, with one servant surviving, but the killers and witness remain unavailable. Oedipus undertakes an investigation, though the opening account states that he unknowingly killed Laius.

l: the plague afflicting Thebes, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: The plague is a disaster afflicting and wasting Thebes, bringing death, damaged crops, failing herds, and fruitless childbirth. According to Apollo's oracle, it is caused by the pollution of Laius's murder and will continue until Laius's murderer is discovered, punished, and removed. Thebes's woes are further increased by Oedipus and Creon's quarrel.

l: Sphinx's riddle, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: The Sphinx's riddle is solved by Oedipus alone through surpassing skill, ending the Sphinx's destruction of Thebes and enabling him to become its protector, king, and Jocasta's husband.

l: Oedipus's former kingship, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: is_received_as_reward_for Sphinx's riddle [after Laius fails to return] Oedipus became king of Thebes after overcoming the Sphinx and being rewarded with the royal scepter. In this unit he acts as the city's protector, promising to investigate Laius's death and restore its welfare.

l: incest, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: is_predicted_by prophecy of parricide and incest [as part of Oedipus's destiny] The opening account states that Oedipus's destiny included incest and that he later married Jocasta, who had been Laius's wife. Oedipus and Jocasta lived together and had four children.

l: parricide, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Parricide is Oedipus’s unwitting killing of Laius, his father, during a quarrel on the road. Foretold as part of Oedipus’s destiny, the act is later recognized by Oedipus and Creon as a crime that makes him accursed, impure, and defiled. Oedipus accepts the deed but stresses that he acted without knowing either identity, under a divine oracle, and claims divine law frees him from guilt.

l: altar of Zeus, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: is_a sacred altar [where the suppliants kneel] The Train of Suppliants gathers before an altar with sacred branches and kneels while seeking Oedipus's help. Oedipus addresses them there and urges them to rise after promising action against the city's affliction.

l: the Cadmeans, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: The Cadmeans are the people inhabiting Thebes. They depend on Oedipus for victory and salvation: he commands them to help expose Laius's murderer, offering favor or punishment, while an oracle says his presence or burial near their land may bring safety or ruin.

l: the murderer of Laius, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: is_exiled_or_slain the land of Thebes [as required by Apollo's oracle] The murderer of Laius is publicly cursed and ordered to leave the land or be expelled. Tiresias declares that the murderer is Oedipus, a man thought to be a foreign sojourner who is actually a true-born Theban.

l: the pollution, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: is_revealed_by the oracle [as the cause requiring expiation] The pollution is said to issue from Laius's death and to be afflicting the land. Oedipus orders the people to drive out the person responsible so that the pollution can be purged.

l: the curse pronounced by Oedipus, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Oedipus pronounces a curse on Laius's murderer: exile from Thebes and human fellowship, denial of shelter, speech, and religious rites, and divine punishment for the killer or concealers. After recalling his actions at the crossroads, he realizes the curse may condemn himself.

l: the Theban throne, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Eteocles seizes the Theban throne from Polynices, who is banished and seeks Argive support to recover power. Oedipus declares that neither the reigning brother nor the exiled brother will retain or regain the throne through his aid.

l: the divine curse on Oedipus, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: drives Oedipus [from the land] The divine curse on Oedipus is associated with the revelation of his crimes and coming ruin. Tiresias says that the God will bring about Oedipus's fall, while Oedipus's father's and mother's curse will drive him from the land.

l: truth, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Truth is portrayed as protected by its own power and compelled into speech by Oedipus's rage; Tiresias says it will expose Oedipus's birth, destruction, and guilt. Dê demands truth from Lichas, whose disclosure explains Heracles's conquest of Oechalia through a maiden's love.

l: Merope, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Merope is Polybus’s consort and queen of Corinth, believed by Oedipus to be his Dorian mother. Oedipus, fearing an oracle’s prophecy of incest with her, flees Corinth, though she is only his believed mother.

l: the Pythian oracle, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: The Pythian oracle is the source of prophecies terrifying Oedipus: it foretells that he will kill his father, Laius, and commit incest with his mother. Oedipus flees Corinth to avoid them, but his killing of an older man and later revelations make the warnings appear true despite temporary doubt after Polybus’s death.

l: the oracle concerning Laius's death, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: Apollo's ministers issue an oracle that Laius's abandoned infant son will kill him; Jocasta later says the son supposedly died and robbers killed Laius, disproving it.

l: Oedipus's killing of Laius and his attendants, The Seven Plays in English Verse
s: occurs_at the crossroad where Laius was killed [during Oedipus's journey from Corinth] Oedipus admits that at a crossroads he encountered an older man in a chariot and attendants who tried to force him from the road. He struck the driver, was struck by the older man, and killed all of them, then fears that the older man was Laius.
